title: Get to know change
hookLine: study how all things change into one another (Meditations 10.11)

cards: Take one photo of the same tree every week for a year, and the strip of pictures tells a story no single photo can. Buds, leaves, gold, bare branches, snow.
It never stops changing; we just don't look closely enough to see it happen. In book ten Marcus treats watching change closely as a discipline of its own, a part of philosophy to train in.

teach.b: Learn the way of looking that sees how all things change into one another, Marcus writes. Keep attending to it, and train yourself in this part of philosophy.

Nothing, he says, is so fitted to produce greatness of mind. Someone who really sees that everything is changing loosens their grip. They stop clutching, because there's nothing to clutch that will hold still.
That person, he says, has in a way already set the body aside, knowing they must leave the human world, no one knows how soon.
They give themselves wholly to justice in what they do, and to the nature of the whole in everything else. What others say or think or do against them doesn't occupy them.
Two things are enough for them: to act justly now, and to be content with what is given now.
And the week, looking back: correct or be kind, the smallest thing, let me not fear, simple and whole, made to bear it, keep the name, and now, study change.
Under all seven lies the same ground: things are moving.
People change, troubles end, prayers turn, names slip and come back. Watch change closely, and you hold everything a little more lightly, and act a little more justly.
Marcus calls that greatness of mind, and he thinks you build it by looking.

how: Some Stoic readers practice contemplating change, watching a flame, a season or their own body, as a way to hold things more lightly and to stay focused on acting justly now.

o: a Greek poet who wrote about the seasons
a Roman gardener who studied trees all year
the emperor who trained himself to watch change

games.q: you notice you're clinging hard to how things are right now. you're Marcus. what's his exercise?
o: watch closely how all things change into one another.
games.why: train yourself, he writes, to see how all things change into each other; it loosens the grip and builds greatness of mind.

practice: If you can, look at something that is changing right now: a cloud, a candle flame, a cup of tea cooling, light moving across a wall, your own breath.
Just watch it change, second by second, and when your mind wanders, come back to the change. Notice how much is happening in what looked still.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who trained himself to watch how all things change into one another, calling it a discipline that builds greatness of mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: change, a turning into something else.

carryVoice: Your line: study change. Nothing holds still, and seeing that loosens the grip. Another week, done.
